n.story:
Your role is transitioning from that of a solitary archive-hunter to a high-level architect of historical narrative. In the past, you spent the majority of your week manually transcribing documents, translating archaic texts, and cross-referencing disparate sources. Now, AI handles the 'brute force' of history—instantly digitizing handwritten manuscripts, identifying patterns across millions of pages of records, and providing initial syntheses of existing literature. This shift liberates you to focus on the deeply human elements of the craft: source criticism, ethical interpretation, and the construction of complex arguments that explain the 'why' behind human events.

As the technical barriers to data access fall, your value lies in your ability to navigate the nuance of bias and cultural context that AI often misses. You will spend more time engaging with the public and policy-makers, using AI-generated visualizations and data models to demonstrate how historical trends inform modern challenges. Your work becomes less about finding the needle in the haystack and more about explaining what the needle tells us about the person who lost it.
